fields.Text: The fourteen extra-alphabetical symbols fall into these kinds: {{c1::short vowels}}, {{c1::pronunciation symbols}}, {{c1::grammatical endings}}, {{c1::spelling variants}}, and {{c1::one consonant that is not in the alphabet chart}}.

fields.Text: The Arabic alphabet contains {{c1::twenty-eight}} letters — consonants and long vowels — plus {{c2::fourteen}} symbols that act as short vowels, pronunciation markers, or grammatical markers.
fields.Back Extra: Cue: letters carry the skeleton; the symbol layer rides above and below it.

decks: all::LIBERTY::LIBERTY FALL 2026::ARAB 101 - Elementary Arabic I::Unit 1::Book Highlights

fields.Text: Formal Arabic has only {{c1::three::how many}} vowel qualities — {{c1::a, i, u}} — each short or long; spoken Arabic adds {{c2::e and o}}.
fields.Back Extra: Cue: vowel length distinguishes emphatic consonants from their plain counterparts — listen for it.

decks: all::LIBERTY::LIBERTY FALL 2026::ARAB 101 - Elementary Arabic I::Unit 1::Book Highlights

fields.Text: Formal Arabic — also called {{c1::Modern Standard}} or {{c1::Classical}} Arabic — is learned {{c2::at school (not at home)}} and is more a {{c2::written}} register than a spoken one.
fields.Back Extra: Cue: you hear it on news broadcasts; educated speakers mix it with dialect in formal settings.

fields.Text: The book's shaami dialogues use the dialect of {{c1::Damascus}}; its maSri is the dialect of {{c2::Cairo}}.

fields.Text:
‎{{c1::ا}}

Name: {{c2::alif}}

Transliteration: {{c2::aa}}

Sound: {{c2::long vowel aa — ranges from e in bet to a in father}}

Connects to the letter after it? {{c1::no — always pick the pen up after it::yes/no}}

Shapes — independent, initial, medial, final:

‎{{c1::ا::independent}}

‎{{c1::ا::initial}}

‎{{c1::ـا::medial}}

‎{{c1::ـا::final}}
fields.Back Extra:
Distinguish: alif is a plain vertical stroke; laam is the same height but sweeps into a bowl at its base.

Shape: one bare upright stroke, no dots — the simplest letter on the chart.

Hook: alif is the exception — every other letter's name opens with its own sound, but alif is a long vowel and carries no consonant.

fields.Text: The Arabic writing system is regularly {{c1::phonetic}}: a one-to-one correspondence between sound and letter — words are written {{c1::the way they are pronounced}}.
fields.Back Extra: Distinguish: English spelling is the opposite — think though / tough / through.

decks: all::LIBERTY::LIBERTY FALL 2026::ARAB 101 - Elementary Arabic I::Unit 1::Book Highlights

fields.Text: In this book's transliteration, emphatic sounds are marked by {{c1::UPPERCASE letters (S vs s)}}, and long vowels by {{c1::doubled vowels (aa, ii, uu)}}.
fields.Back Extra: Ex: S = emphatic ص while s = plain س; aa is held longer than a.

decks: all::LIBERTY::LIBERTY FALL 2026::ARAB 101 - Elementary Arabic I::Unit 1::Book Highlights

fields.Text: Levantine pronunciation sometimes uses a very short, unstressed {{c1::schwa}} sound (ə).
fields.Back Extra: Ex: the e in listen.

decks: all::LIBERTY::LIBERTY FALL 2026::ARAB 101 - Elementary Arabic I::Unit 1::Book Highlights

fields.Text: Arabic is written and read from {{c1::right to left}}.
fields.Back Extra: Cue: books and magazines open the "other way" from English ones.

decks: all::LIBERTY::LIBERTY FALL 2026::ARAB 101 - Elementary Arabic I::Unit 1::Book Highlights

fields.Text: The vowelling layer (vocalization) is normally {{c1::omitted}} in written Arabic — readers recognize words {{c1::without it}}.
fields.Back Extra: Pitfall: your textbook prints vowels while you learn; newspapers will not.

decks: all::LIBERTY::LIBERTY FALL 2026::ARAB 101 - Elementary Arabic I::Unit 1::Book Highlights

fields.Text: Arabic letters are connected {{c1::in both print AND script}} — unlike Latin letters, which connect only in handwriting.
fields.Back Extra: Why: this is why letters change shape by position — they must join their neighbors.

decks: all::LIBERTY::LIBERTY FALL 2026::ARAB 101 - Elementary Arabic I::Unit 1::Book Highlights

fields.Text: "{{c1::Initial}} position" = the letter is not connected to a previous letter; "{{c2::medial}} position" = the letter sits between two other letters.
fields.Back Extra: Cue: Unit 1 teaches only the independent (isolated) forms — position variants come in Units 2-10.

decks: all::LIBERTY::LIBERTY FALL 2026::ARAB 101 - Elementary Arabic I::Unit 1::Book Highlights

fields.Text: Polite behavior requires you to say hello to {{c1::everyone in a room or place you enter}} — including a loosely defined {{c1::"space" someone regularly occupies}}.
fields.Back Extra:
Ex: an outdoor work area, or a guard's position outside a building.

Cue: entering = greeting; the room does not have to have walls.

Transliteration: {{c1::maa}}

{{c2::what?}} — the question word used before a NOUN: "___ ismuka?"
fields.Back Extra:
Cue: MSA — maa

Pitfall: maa only goes with a noun — "what's your NAME". Verbs take a different word, which she is saving for later. Her line: "maa comes with a noun only."

Distinguish: Levantine says shuu — shuu ismak? "Even in Saudi Arabia they used to say shuu. Everybody knows shuu."

fields.Text: Vowel quality is {{c1::which particular sound a vowel has}}.
fields.Back Extra:
Ex: "The pronunciation of alif has a similar range; we refer to these differences in pronunciation as vowel quality."

Distinguish: vowel quality is which sound the vowel is — the e of bet, the a of bat, the u of but; vowel length is how long the vowel is held.

Why: two things shift the quality of alif — the speaker's regional dialect (deeper, like father, in the Arabian Peninsula and Iraq; more frontal, toward the e of bet, in North Africa) and the surrounding consonants.

fields.Text: Besides vowel quality, Arabic also distinguishes vowel {{c1::length}}, and this too can change a word's meaning.
fields.Back Extra:
Ex: DHaalim — a long alif in the first syllable, a short i in the second.

Distinguish: quality is which vowel sound you make (a frontal or a deep alif); length is how long you hold it — Arabic keeps track of both.

Cue: alif itself is a long vowel — the one you hear held in DHaalim.

decks: all::LIBERTY::LIBERTY FALL 2026::ARAB 101 - Elementary Arabic I::Unit 2::Book Highlights

fields.Text: In Arabic, word stress is attracted to the syllable with a {{c1::long::long or short}} vowel.
fields.Back Extra:
Ex: DHaalim — the accent falls on the first syllable, the one with the long alif, not on the short i of the second.

Distinguish: vowel length is a property of one vowel (long or short); word stress is a property of the whole word (which syllable carries the accent).
